judge_assessment.explanation: ACCEPT is right and I could not fault the mathematics. Working from the worksheet and verify.json: problem 1 shows a ten-frame with 6 dots and asks 6 + __ = 10 (4); problem 2 is 3 + __ = 10 (7); 3 is 10 − 8 = 2; 4 is 7 + __ = 10 (3); 5 is 8 on the frame with 4 in hand, (a) 2 and (b) 12; 6 is 10 − 6 = 4; 7 is the bond 10/2 giving 8; 8 is 7 + 5 with (a) 3 and (b) 12; 9 is 10 seats with (a) 6 and (b) 3; 10 is (a) 7 then (b) 13. Every one matches. One note on the judge's phrasing: its list '10, 10, 2, 10, 12, ...' recites the completed equation for the make-ten items rather than the missing addend the child writes (4, 7 and 3), which is defensible since the worksheet prints '6 + __ = 10', but it is not the verified expected value and it makes the recitation harder to check against the bank. Nothing in the verdict is contradicted by the artifacts. The judge did not catch the one defect I found, in the study guide's third try-it.

strengths_to_preserve: This is the batch's model case for answer-slot coverage: problems 5, 8, 9 and 10 are each split into (a) and (b), and verify.json gives each part its OWN entry (14 entries for 10 problems), so every blank the child fills is independently machine-checked and appears in the bank ('5. 2, 12', '9. 6, 3', '10. 7, 13'). Three other cases in this batch print sub-part slots with a single entry; this one shows the correct pattern already exists.

The sheet is built on one idea seen three ways and says so in the key: 'problems 1, 4 and 7 are the same idea in three pictures — a frame, a story and a bond. Say so out loud; that is the connection the sheet is building.' Interleaving here is conceptual rather than merely shuffled.

Problem 10 is a genuine two-step synthesis (give 3 away from 10, then add 6 by making a ten again) and the key insists on the method rather than the number: 'full credit for any correct method, but ask the child to show the ten.'

The declared trap on problem 5 (answer 10, from filling the frame and forgetting the counters still in hand) is the exact error the make-ten method produces, is machine-proved distinguishable, and the study guide's closing watch-out box repeats it ('check your hand — is it empty?').

root_causes.description: The study guide's third try-it prints a parenthetical hint that is phrased as a question with a different answer from the printed check. The item reads 'Try it: 8 + 5 (how many does 8 need to make ten?)' and the upside-down check reads '13'. The parenthetical is intended as scaffolding toward the decomposition, but it is the last question on the line, and its answer is 2. A five- or six-year-old who answers the question as written will self-check against a number that does not correspond to it. The other five study-guide try-its ask exactly one thing.
evidence: evals/runs/curriculum-shardX-20260803T181926Z/tasks/curr-020/study_guide.tex line 81: '\textbf{Try it:} \quad $8 + 5$ \quad (how many does $8$ need to make ten?)' with the printed check '13'.

verify_study_guide.json id 6: {'type': 'eval', 'expr': 'a + b', 'at': {'a': 8, 'b': 5}, 'expected': 13, 'role': 'tryit'} — only the sum is checked, so the printed hint-question has no answer anywhere in the packet.
The parallel try-its in sections 1 and 2 ('4 + __ = 10', check 6; '10 − 2 =', check 8) each ask a single question whose answer is the check.

improvements.title: Phrase study-guide try-it scaffolding as an instruction, not as a question with a different answer
improvements.proposed_change: Rewrite the hint so it cannot be mistaken for the thing being asked: 'Try it: 8 + 5 (make the ten first)' or '(start by filling the frame from the 5)'. Then generalise it in SKILL.md's study-guide section: a try-it may carry at most one interrogative, and any scaffolding must be imperative. Enforce it cheaply in tests/check_study_guide.py, which already parses tryitbox contents — fail (or warn) when a tryitbox contains more than one '?' and the box has a single verify entry, since that is precisely the shape where the printed check can answer the wrong question.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture study-guide .tex with a tryitbox reading 'Try it: $8+5$ (how many does $8$ need to make ten?)' bound to a single verify entry expecting 13: assert check_study_guide.py flags the box and names the second question. Rewrite the parenthetical as '(make the ten first)' and assert it is silent. Today the box passes untouched, so the first assertion fails before the fix.
improvements.expected_impact: A child using the upside-down check gets confirmation of the question they were actually asked. Small, but the try-it is the one place in the packet designed for unsupervised self-checking, so a mismatch there costs more than its size suggests.
improvements.risk: Low. Counting question marks is crude and will occasionally flag a legitimate two-part try-it; ship it as a warning, and note that a genuinely two-part try-it should carry two verify entries under the same id, which is the same rule the worksheet side needs.

case_summary: A correct, well-structured make-ten packet and a deserved ACCEPT. All 14 verified values check out against the worksheet, and this is the one case in my batch that gets multi-part answer coverage right — every (a)/(b) slot on problems 5, 8, 9 and 10 has its own verify entry and its own bank row, which is exactly the pattern curr-024, curr-028 and curr-031 are missing. The interleaving is conceptual (frame, story, bond as three pictures of one idea, said out loud in the key) and the closing two-step story earns its place. The only defect I found is in the study guide: the third try-it reads '8 + 5 (how many does 8 need to make ten?)' with the check printed as 13, so the parenthetical hint is a question whose own answer is 2. That is polish, not correctness, but it sits in the one box a child is meant to check unsupervised. I also note the judge's answer list recites the completed equation totals ('10') for the make-ten items rather than the missing addends (4, 7, 3) — defensible, but not what verify.json records.
